doc.title: Eddie Miller and Pete Fountain Interview, 1970-01-09

title: Sitting in with George Lewis and Tony Almerico; black and white musicians
summary: Pete sat in as a teen with George Lewis and at Tony Almerico's room, and says musicians were first to integrate.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That brings up a question. I wonder, do white and black musicians, do they have much influence on each other? Does it cross the racial lines as far as musical influence is concerned?
I think they do, because I used to sit in with George Lewis when I was a kid, and this goes back, well, I'm Jack Benny's age now. I'm 39. I'll stay this year for a couple years. I mean, this day.
He had a tremendous talent, didn't he?

But, oh, fantastic. And his band used to play a place they call Across the Tracks on Manny's. Really, I don't remember the name. I just remember how I used to get there, either by bus or something, and they were so great. They let me sit in to let a kid, you know, when you say 15, 16 years old, sit on 14, I think I was between 14 and 16 years old. And another one was that helped, well, Tony Almerico really did a wonderful job with kids. But we don't have, you don't have that place, any places like that to where you can take the kids, because you have to be, what, 18.
Tony Almerico had that music room down in Wall Street.
Right, right, the Parisian room. That was a great influence on me, and a lot of kids, like the Dukes of Dixieland, and, you know, Frank and Fred Asunto.
What do you think about that, Eddie, about the influence between white and black musicians?

Oh, I think this is one of the first things that happened, I think, you speak about this, about integration. I think that musicians, white and black, they were the first to get together, and there was never any... Oh, look at Lloyd. Just always, since I was a kid, I mean, there was no way there was any color situation in any way.
